3.1: We ought to consider not only that our life is wasting away day by day and a smaller part of it is left, but another thing must also be taken into account: that if a man should live longer, it is quite uncertain whether the understanding will still be adequate for grasping things, and keep the power of contemplation which strives to gain knowledge of the divine and the human. For if he begins to fall into senility, perspiration and nutrition and imagination and appetite, and whatever else there is of the kind, will not fail; but the power of making use of ourselves, and filling up the measure of our duty, and clearly distinguishing all appearances, and considering whether a man should now leave life, and whatever else of the kind absolutely requires a disciplined reason—all this is already extinguished. We must hurry, then, not only because we are nearer to death every day, but also because the conception and understanding of things cease first.
3.2: We ought to observe also that even the things which follow on from the things produced according to nature contain something pleasing and attractive. For instance, when bread is baked, some parts split at the surface, and these parts which open in this way, and have a certain form contrary to the purpose of the baker's craft, are beautiful in a way, and in a particular way stir a desire to eat. And again, figs, when they are quite ripe, gape open; and in ripe olives the very fact that they are close to rotting adds a particular beauty to the fruit. And the ears of corn bending down, and the lion's brows, and the foam which flows from the mouths of wild boars, and many other things—though they are far from beautiful if a man examines them one by one—still, because they follow from the things formed by nature, help to adorn them, and they please the mind; so that if a man has a feeling for, and a deeper insight into, the things which are produced in the universe, there is hardly one of those which follow as a consequence which will not seem to him to be arranged in a way that gives pleasure. And so he will see even the real gaping jaws of wild beasts with no less pleasure than those which painters and sculptors show in imitation; and in an old woman and an old man he will be able to see a certain maturity and grace; and he will be able to look on the attractive loveliness of the young with chaste eyes; and many such things will present themselves, pleasing not to every man, but only to him who has become truly familiar with Nature and her works.
3.3: Hippocrates, after curing many diseases, himself fell sick and died. The Chaldaei foretold the deaths of many, and then fate caught them too. Alexander and Pompeius, and Caius Caesar, after so often utterly destroying whole cities, and cutting to pieces many tens of thousands of cavalry and infantry in battle, themselves too at last departed from life. Heraclitus, after so many speculations on the conflagration of the universe, was filled with water internally and died smeared all over with mud. And lice destroyed Democritus; and other lice killed Socrates. What does all this mean? You have embarked, you have made the voyage, you have come to shore; get out. If indeed to another life, there is no lack of gods, not even there; but if to a state without sensation, you will cease to be held by pains and pleasures, and to be a slave to the vessel, which is as much inferior as that which serves it is superior: for the one is intelligence and divinity; the other is earth and decay.
3.4: Do not waste the rest of your life in thoughts about others, when you do not direct your thoughts to some object of common benefit. For you lose the opportunity of doing something else when you have thoughts such as these: What is so-and-so doing, and why, and what is he saying, and what is he thinking about, and what is he plotting, and whatever else of the kind makes us wander away from observing our own ruling power. We ought, then, to check in the series of our thoughts everything that is aimless and useless, but most of all the over-curious and the malicious; and a man should accustom himself to think only of those things about which, if someone should suddenly ask, What is in your thoughts now? you could immediately answer with perfect openness, This or That; so that from your words it would be plain that everything in you is simple and kindly, and such as befits a social animal, and one that does not care at all for thoughts about pleasure or sensual enjoyments, nor has any rivalry or envy and suspicion, or anything else you would blush to say you had in your mind. For the man who is like this, and no longer delays being among the number of the best, is like a priest and minister of the gods, making use too of the god which is planted within him, which keeps the man unstained by pleasure, unharmed by any pain, untouched by any insult, feeling no wrong, a fighter in the noblest fight, one who cannot be overpowered by any passion, dyed deep with justice, accepting with all his soul everything which happens and is assigned to him as his portion; and not often, nor without great necessity and for the general good, imagining what another says, or does, or thinks. For it is only what belongs to himself that he makes the material for his activity; and he constantly thinks of what is allotted to himself out of the sum total of things, and he makes his own acts fair, and he is convinced that his own portion is good. For the lot which is assigned to each man is carried along with him and carries him along with it. And he remembers also that every rational animal is his kinsman, and that to care for all men is according to man's nature; and a man should hold on to the opinion not of all, but only of those who admittedly live according to nature. But as for those who do not live so, he always bears in mind what kind of men they are both at home and away from home, both by night and by day, and what they are, and with what men they live an impure life. Accordingly, he does not value at all the praise which comes from such men, since they are not even satisfied with themselves.
3.5: Work not unwillingly, nor without regard for the common good, nor without due thought, nor while distracted; don't let elaborate ornament dress up your thoughts, and be neither a man of many words nor busy with too many things. And further, let the god that is in you be the guardian of a living being who is manly and mature, engaged in public affairs, a Roman, and a ruler, who has taken his post like a man waiting for the signal that calls him from life, and ready to go, needing neither oath nor anyone's testimony. Be cheerful too, and don't look for outside help, or the peace that others give. A man, then, must stand upright, not be held upright by others.
3.6: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, temperance, fortitude, and, in a word, anything better than your own mind's satisfaction with the things which it enables you to do according to right reason, and with the condition that is assigned to you without your own choice; if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with all your soul, and enjoy what you have found to be the best. But if nothing appears to be better than the god which is planted in you, which has brought all your appetites under its control, and carefully examines all impressions, and, as Socrates said, has detached itself from the persuasions of the senses, and has submitted itself to the gods, and cares for mankind; if you find everything else smaller and of less value than this, give way to nothing else; for if you once turn aside and lean towards it, you will no longer be able, without distraction, to give preference to that good thing which is properly yours and your own; for it is not right that anything of any other kind, such as praise from the many, or power, or enjoyment of pleasure, should compete with what is rationally and politically, or practically, good. All these things, even though they may seem to fit in with the better things to a small degree, suddenly gain the upper hand and carry us away. But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better, and hold to it.—But what is useful is the better.—Well, then, if it is useful to you as a rational being, keep to it; but if it is only useful to you as an animal, say so, and maintain your judgement without arrogance: only take care that you make the inquiry by a sound method.
3.7: Never value anything as profitable to yourself which will force you to break your promise, to lose your self-respect, to hate any man, to suspect, to curse, to act the hypocrite, to desire anything which needs walls and curtains: for he who has preferred his own intelligence and the spirit within, and the worship of its excellence, to everything else, plays no tragic part, does not groan, and will need neither solitude nor much company; and, most important of all, he will live without either pursuing death or fleeing from it; and whether his soul is to be enclosed in the body for a longer or a shorter time, he does not care at all: for even if he must depart immediately, he will go as readily as if he were going to do anything else which can be done with decency and order; taking care of this only, all through life, that his thoughts do not turn away from anything which belongs to an intelligent animal and a member of a civic community.
3.8: In the mind of one who is disciplined and purified you will find no corrupt matter, nor impurity, nor any sore skinned over. Nor is his life incomplete when fate overtakes him, as one might say of an actor who leaves the stage before the play is ended and finished. Besides, there is nothing in him servile, nor affected, nor too closely bound to other things, nor yet detached from them, nothing deserving blame, nothing which seeks a hiding place.
3.9: Revere the faculty which produces opinion. On this faculty it depends entirely whether there will exist in your ruling part any opinion inconsistent with nature and with the makeup of the rational animal. And this faculty promises freedom from hasty judgement, and friendship towards men, and obedience to the gods.
3.10: Throwing away, then, all things, hold only to these, which are few; and besides, bear in mind that every man lives only this present time, which is an indivisible point, and that all the rest of his life is either past or uncertain. Short, then, is the time which every man lives; and small the corner of the earth where he lives; and short too is the longest fame after death, and even this is only kept up by a succession of poor human beings, who will very soon die, and who do not even know themselves, much less him who died long ago.
3.11: To the aids which have been mentioned let this one still be added: make for yourself a definition or description of the thing which is presented to you, so as to see clearly what kind of thing it is in its substance, stripped bare, as a complete whole, and tell yourself its proper name, and the names of the things of which it has been made up, and into which it will be broken down. For nothing produces greatness of mind so much as being able to examine methodically and truly every object which is presented to you in life, and always to look at things so as to see at the same time what kind of universe this is, and what kind of use everything serves in it, and what value everything has with reference to the whole, and what with reference to man, who is a citizen of the highest city, of which all other cities are like families; what each thing is, and what it is made of, and how long it is in the nature of this thing which now makes an impression on me to last, and what virtue I need with respect to it, such as gentleness, manliness, truth, faithfulness, simplicity, contentment, and the rest. Therefore, on every occasion a man should say: This comes from god; and this is according to the allotment and spinning of the thread of destiny, and such-like coincidence and chance; and this is from one of the same stock, a kinsman and partner, one who does not know, however, what is according to his nature. But I know; for this reason I behave towards him with kindness and justice, according to the natural law of fellowship. At the same time, however, in things indifferent I try to determine the value of each.
3.12: If you work at what is in front of you, following right reason seriously, vigorously, calmly, without allowing anything else to distract you, but keeping your divine part pure, as if you were bound to give it back immediately; if you hold to this, expecting nothing, fearing nothing, but satisfied with your present activity according to nature, and with heroic truth in every word and sound you utter, you will live happily. And there is no man who is able to prevent this.
3.13: As physicians always have their instruments and knives ready for cases which suddenly require their skill, so you should have principles ready for understanding things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest thing, with a remembrance of the bond which unites the divine and the human to one another. For you will not do anything well which concerns man without at the same time referring it to things divine; nor the reverse.
3.14: No longer wander aimlessly; for you will not read your own memoirs, nor the deeds of the ancient Romans and Hellenes, and the selections from books which you were saving for your old age. Hurry, then, to the end which you have before you, and, throwing away idle hopes, come to your own aid, if you care at all for yourself, while it is in your power.
3.15: They do not know how many things are meant by the words stealing, sowing, buying, keeping quiet, seeing what ought to be done; for this is not done by the eyes, but by another kind of vision.
3.16: Body, soul, intelligence: to the body belong sensations, to the soul appetites, to the intelligence principles. To receive the impressions of forms by means of appearances belongs even to animals; to be pulled by the strings of desire belongs both to wild beasts and to men who have made themselves into women, and to a Phalaris and a Nero; and to have the intelligence that guides towards the things which appear suitable belongs also to those who do not believe in the gods, and who betray their country, and do their impure deeds once they have shut the doors. If, then, everything else is common to all that I have mentioned, there remains what is peculiar to the good man: to be pleased and content with what happens, and with the thread which is spun for him; and not to defile the divinity which is planted in his breast, nor disturb it with a crowd of images, but to keep it tranquil, following it obediently as a god, neither saying anything contrary to the truth, nor doing anything contrary to justice. And if all men refuse to believe that he lives a simple, modest, and contented life, he is neither angry with any of them, nor does he stray from the road which leads to the end of life, to which a man ought to come pure, tranquil, ready to depart, and without any compulsion perfectly reconciled to his lot.
